comment: What update-languages.py bundles: VS Code's built-in language data at one commit, plus grammars VS Code does not ship, each pinned to a commit of its upstream repository. Licences are read at the same commits.

unresolvedIncludes.comment: Scopes bundled grammars include that are not bundled, and why. A rule that includes one of them matches nothing, as in VS Code without that extension.

scopes.source.abap: Markdown fences of ABAP; VS Code ships no grammar for it either.

fenceAliases.comment: Markdown fence words the Markdown grammars do not know, for shell sessions as GitHub writes them. Each becomes the language named.

provenance.comment: Grammars VS Code ships without an information_for_contributors note naming their upstream.

licenses.comment: Where each upstream's licence is written. A TextMate bundle has its licence in the README's License section.

atom/language-java.note: VS Code's last copy converted from this repository (microsoft/vscode b37252c); VS Code now takes Java from redhat-developer/vscode-java, an EPL-2.0 repository.

jeff-hykin/better-cpp-syntax.note: Taken at 06f4011, which only changes LICENSE back to MIT from the GPL-3.0 the repository carried from 2023 to May 2026; the grammar is the one VS Code pins (071dd6e).

grammarFiles.comment: Grammars bundled from another commit than the one contributing them. Java: VS Code's grammar today comes from redhat-developer/vscode-java, an EPL-2.0 repository; this is VS Code's last copy converted from atom/language-java (MIT), so its licence is beyond doubt. C++: the commit VS Code pins (071dd6e) falls in the time the repository was GPL-3.0 (2023 to May 2026); the next commit, 06f4011, changes only LICENSE back to MIT, so the same grammar is taken from there.
